analysis.one_liner: Requires immediate federal oil and gas lease sales and blocks any delays or moratoria.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee at the end of the 117th Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the President to immediately hold oil and gas lease sales on federal lands and offshore waters, and barred the administration from delaying any related drilling permits, approvals, or authorizations unless Congress itself authorized the delay. It also would have rescinded the portion of Executive Order 14008 directing federal agencies to tackle the climate crisis by ending new federal oil and gas leasing. The bill was referred to the Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees, sent to a subcommittee, and never advanced further before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that drill on federal land and offshore waters. The bill would guarantee a steady supply of new federal leases and strip the administration's ability to slow or pause permitting, removing regulatory friction and lowering the cost of securing drilling access. Rescinding Section 208 of Executive Order 14008 would restore leasing as a default on federal lands.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the President to 'immediately and without delay' hold federal onshore and offshore oil and gas lease sales, and forbids any action that would prohibit or delay the issuance of leases, permits, approvals, or authorizations on federal land unless Congress authorized it [S3].

Section 2 rescinds Section 208 of Executive Order 14008, the directive to pause new oil and gas leasing on federal lands as part of addressing the climate crisis, removing the legal basis for that pause [S3].

The bill covers national forest lands, public lands, and the outer continental shelf, but excludes national parks and most wildlife refuges, so it would reopen a broad swath of federal territory to leasing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the public would bear the environmental costs of expanded federal drilling — more greenhouse gas emissions, more land disturbance, and loss of the administration's authority to pause federal leasing — while taxpayers would receive oil and gas revenue from leases at the pace the bill mandates. Consumers could see some downward pressure on energy prices from increased supply, though the federal share of production is modest and price effects are uncertain.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through environmental costs of drilling

drawbacks.text: Rescinding the leasing pause in Executive Order 14008 removes a tool the administration had identified for reducing greenhouse gas emissions from federal lands, where fossil fuel production is a significant emissions source [S3].

The bill is unusual in that it strips the President of discretion over leasing and permitting on federal land and offshore waters, requiring sales 'immediately and without delay' and allowing no administrative delays of any kind unless Congress itself authorizes a pause [S3].

Mandating lease sales regardless of market demand can result in leases sold at low prices that go undeveloped, which reduces federal revenue relative to what competitive, demand-responsive sales would bring [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main effect is to guarantee drilling access on federal lands and offshore waters for oil and gas producers by removing the administration's ability to slow or pause leasing and permitting. That could modestly increase domestic supply, but it comes by permanently handing a concentrated industry a favored position on publicly owned land and undoing a climate directive, with the environmental costs falling on the public. It offered little in return for taxpayers beyond standard lease receipts.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee — referred to Natural Resources and Agriculture and then to a Conservation and Forestry subcommittee — and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 5, 2022 by Rep. Michael Burgess and referred to the House Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees [S1] [S5].
On April 18, 2022, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Conservation and Forestry, and no further action was taken [S5].
The bill drew zero cosponsors during its time in Congress [S4].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without the bill receiving any vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a new policy, but oil and gas drillers are no worse off and the administration's authority to pause federal leasing survived, along with the climate directive the bill targeted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The leasing pause and climate directive survived intact

for.name: Rep. Michael C. Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require immediate federal oil and gas lease sales and rescind the federal leasing pause, but recruited no cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors, so no party breakdown exists; the only sponsor was a Republican.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land and offshore waters
industries.note: The bill would have guaranteed a continuous flow of new federal leases and barred any delay of drilling permits, removing regulatory friction for drillers operating on land owned by the public. Its benefits would have flowed to leaseholders while the environmental costs of expanded drilling fell on everyone.

Mandated lease sales would generate federal royalty and bonus revenue, which flows back to taxpayers and affected states. But the bill also removed the administration's ability to weigh environmental and other public values before opening federal land to drilling.

Expanded leasing on national forest and public lands, though excluding national parks and most wildlife refuges, would open more territory to drilling activity and its associated disturbance, working against groups that use and protect those lands.
